## {{< iconify noto-v1 package >}} Setting up R Packages



```{r}
#| label: setup
#| echo: true
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| 
library(tidyverse)   
library(ggformula)
library(sysfonts)    ## use custom fonts (need to be installed on your OS)  
library(systemfonts) # Thomas Pederson's recent font management package
library(showtext)    ## add google fonts to plots
library(ggtext)      ## add improved text rendering to ggplot2
##
library(ggrepel)     ## Text-repelled labels
library(marquee)     ## Annotations with fonts in ggplot

```


We may have been using `ggplot2` for a while now, but there is always more to learn about the aesthetics of our plots. In this module, we will explore how to use different fonts and themes to make our plots look more polished and professional. 

## Using Preferred Fonts

We may prefer specific fonts for **our plots**. (And we may also want to use these fonts on our websites, which we will examine in the next Module on [Branding and Typography for Websites](../40-Branding/index.qmd)).)


These are the steps to using fonts for **charts** in R: 

1. Selecting the Fonts
1. Downloading the chosen Fonts
1. Specifying the chosen Fonts in `ggplot` themes
1. Using the themes in `ggplot` charts

Let us look at these steps!

### Step 1: Selecting Fonts

There is a nice website called [Font Pair](https://fontpair.co/all) that suggests **elegant pairs of fonts** that you may use for Website Headings and Body Text. Then we can obtain these chosen fonts from [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/).

### Step 2: Live Downloading Fonts from Google

[The easiest way]{style="background-color:yellow;"} to get fonts is **live downloading of fonts** from Google Fonts. 

Let us add a handful of fonts to our R session. We will use the `sysfonts::font_add_google()` function from the `sysfonts` package to download Google fonts into our session. These fonts will then be included into our session using `showtext::showtext_auto()`.

A typical code chunk to do this could look like: 

```{{r}}
#| label: live-download-google-fonts

## Clean the slate
systemfonts::clear_local_fonts()
systemfonts::clear_registry()

# Add three Google Fonts
# Arguments: font family name, Google Font name
font_add_google("Roboto Condensed", "Roboto Condensed")
font_add_google("Lato", "Lato")
font_add_google("Alegreya", "Alegreya")

## Enable these fonts
showtext_auto() # set these fonts as default for the session

## Optional Check, comment out this line in production code
sysfonts::font_families() # check which fonts are available in the session

```

Ensure that you use the right `name` for the font family, as shown above. It is text-sensitive. The `family` is up to you to choose. Using similar names for `name` and `family` is a good idea, as shown above.

### Step 3: Specifying the `ggplot` Plot Theme

Now that we have the fonts installed, we need to set our ggplot theme to use these fonts. 

But, what are these `theme` elements?

```{r}
#| label: fig-ggplot-theme-elements
#| echo: FALSE
#| fig.alt: "ggplot2 Theme Elements. Source: Rosana Ferrero on Twitter, Sept 11, 2022"
#| fig.cap: "ggplot2 Theme Elements. Source: Rosana Ferrero, on Twitter Sept 11, 2022"
#| 
knitr::include_graphics("../../../../../materials/images/ggplot_theme_elements.jfif")

```
So now that we understand the elements of the themes, let us set our ggplot theme.

::: callout-note
### Fonts in ggplot

Using `showtext(auto)` as shown above allows us to modify the ***non-graph*** elements of the ggplot chart: the `axes`, the `title`, the `legend` etc. 

If we wish to add text with fonts to the body of the chart itself, as with geoms such as `text`and `label` annotations , we need to do one more thing: use `update_geom_defaults()` as shown below:

:::


###### Fonts for Non-graphical Elements

First we set the fonts for the ***non-graphical*** elements in ggplot, such as `title`, `subtitle`, `axis title`, and `legend title` for example:

```{{r}}
#| label: set-ggplot2-theme
#| 

theme_madhatter <- function(){ 

    theme_bw(base_size = 10) + # Base Theme, Black-White
    
    theme_sub_axis(title = element_text(family = "Roboto Condensed", 
                                       size = 8),
                   text = element_text(family = "Roboto Condensed", 
                                       size = 6)) + 
    
    theme_sub_legend(text = element_text(family = "Roboto Condensed", 
                                         size = 6),
                     title = element_text(family = "Montserrat", 
                                          size = 8)) + 
    
    theme_sub_plot(title = element_text(family = "Montserrat", 
                                        size = 14, face = "bold"),
                   title.position = "plot",
                   subtitle = element_text(family = "Montserrat", 
                                           size = 10),
                   caption = element_text(family = "Montserrat", 
                                          size = 6),
                   caption.position = "plot")
    
}

## Set the theme
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_madhatter())

```

###### Setting fonts for Chart Elements

We now need to enable to use of these fonts ***inside*** the chart area of ggplot, say in `annotations`, `text` geoms, `label` geoms, and `marquee` geoms.

```{{r}}
#| label: set-geom-default-font
#| 


## Use available fonts in ggplot label and text within the ggplot geoms 
ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text", new = list(
  family = "Roboto Condensed",
  face = "plain",
  size = 8/ggplot2::.pt, # Converting points to "mm" default
  color = "#2b2b2b"
)
)
ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label", new = list(
  family = "Roboto Condensed",
  face = "plain",
  size = 8/ggplot2::.pt, # Converting points to "mm" default
  color = "#2b2b2b"
)
)

```

### Final Step: Using the Fonts!!

***Where do we put all these code chunks floating around??!!!***

Quarto now has a feature that includes a`_setup.qmd` at the root of your Project. These code chunks, preferably in **one single code chunk**, can be pasted into this file, and this file invoked at the start of each new Quarto document using:

`{{< include /_setup.qmd >}}`

A sample `_setup.qmd` format, with quite some detail, is embedded below for your copying pleasure:

```{{r}}

#| label: setup-site
#| include: false
#| cache: false

# Install/load packages if needed
if (!requireNamespace("showtext", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("showtext")
}
if (!requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  install.packages("ggplot2")
}

library(showtext)
library(ggplot2)

# Add three Google Fonts
# Arguments: font family name, Google Font name
font_add_google("Roboto Condensed", "Roboto Condensed")
font_add_google("Lato", "Lato")
font_add_google("Alegreya", "Alegreya")

# Tell R to use showtext for all subsequent plots
showtext_auto()

# Optional: set DPI for raster devices (adjust if you need high-res PNGs)
showtext_opts(dpi = 300)

# Set a site-wide ggplot theme using the loaded fonts
ggplot2::theme_set(
  ggplot2::theme_bw(
    base_size = 14,
    base_family = "Roboto Condensed"
  )
)

## Set the ggplot theme
theme_madhatter <- function(base_size = 10, exhibit = TRUE) {
  th <- ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = base_size) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.margin = ggplot2::margin(t = 1, r = 2, b = 1, l = 1, unit = "cm"),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_text(
        family = "Roboto Condensed",
        size = 10
      ),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(
        family = "Roboto Condensed",
        size = 8
      ),
      legend.text = ggplot2::element_text(
        family = "Roboto Condensed",
        size = 6
      ),
      legend.title = ggplot2::element_text(
        family = "Alegreya",
        size = 8
      ),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(
        family = "Alegreya",
        size = 14,
        face = "bold"
      ),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      plot.subtitle = ggplot2::element_text(
        family = "Alegreya",
        size = 10
      ),
      plot.caption = ggplot2::element_text(
        family = "Alegreya",
        size = 6
      ),
      plot.caption.position = "plot"
    )}

## Set the theme for all plots
ggplot2::theme_set(theme_madhatter())

## Update the fonts for geoms as well!
## Use available fonts in ggplot label and text within the ggplot geoms 
ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "text", new = list(
  family = "Roboto Condensed",
  face = "plain",
  size = 8/ggplot2::.pt, # Converting 8 points to "mm" default
  color = "#2b2b2b"
)
)
ggplot2::update_geom_defaults(geom = "label", new = list(
  family = "Roboto Condensed",
  face = "plain",
  size = 8/ggplot2::.pt, # Converting 8 points to "mm" default
  color = "#2b2b2b"
)
)


```

NOTE: this code chunk is **all** that is meant to be in the file `_setup.qmd`. ***There is nothing else, no YAML header, no sections, no text. Just one code chunk***. 

## Does it all work??

Let us quickly see the results of using this `_setup.qmd`. We will compare a plain, basic plot, with one achieved after invoking `_setup.qmd`. 

#### Data

We will work with a **familiar** dataset, so that we can concentrate on the chart aesthetics, without having to spend time getting used to the data: the `penguins` dataset again, now part of the R installation!

```{r}
#| label: tbl-read-penguins-data
#| tbl-cap: "Penguins Dataset"
#| message: false
#| echo: false
#| 
data(penguins, package = "datasets")
penguins <- penguins %>% drop_na() # remove data containing missing data

## Create a nicely formatted table
## uses `kableExtra` package
## 
penguins %>% 
  kableExtra::kbl(caption = "Penguins Dataset") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_paper(full_width = FALSE,
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "responsive"),
    position = "center") %>%
  kableExtra::scroll_box(height = "350px")

```


#### Basic Plot

A basic scatter plot first, which we will decorate with fonts:

```{r}
#| label: fig-basic-scatter-plot
#| fig.cap: "Vanilla Scatter plot"
#| code-fold: true
#| 

penguins %>% drop_na() %>% 
  gf_point(body_mass ~ flipper_len, colour = ~ species, size = 2) %>% 
  gf_labs(title = "My Penguin Plot", x = "Flipper Length", y = "Body Mass (gms)") %>% 
  gf_refine(annotate(geom = "text", label = "Important\n Points", x = 220, y = 3500),
            annotate(geom = "rect", xmin = 200, xmax = 210, ymin = 3000, ymax = 5700, alpha = .2),
            annotate('curve',x = 220, y = 3200,yend = 3000,xend = 205,
    linewidth = 1, curvature = -0.5, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, 'cm')))) %>%
  
  ## Labels and Title
  gf_labs(
    title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins (Pygoscelis)',
    subtitle = 'A scatter plot of bill depth versus bill length.',
    caption = 'Data: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014) PLoS ONE',
    x = 'Bill Length (mm)', 
    y = 'Bill Depth (mm)',
    color = 'Body mass (g)'
  ) %>%
  gf_theme(theme = theme_grey())

```

We see that the ggplot theme uses the basic fonts from the `theme_grey()`, ***the default theme in `ggplot`***. And here below, is the same chart achieved with our new theme, which was set using the `_setup.qmd()` from above. This is from the [Project Peasants Website](https://project-peasants.netlify.app/classwork/day1/index.html) which uses the `_setup.qmd` file to set the fonts for all plots on the website.)

{{< include /_setup.qmd >}}

```{r}
#| label: fig-themed-ggplot
#| fig-cap: "Plot themed with _setup.qmd"
#| echo: false

knitr::include_graphics("https://project-peasants.netlify.app/classwork/day1/index_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png")
```

## Wait, but Why?

- Using appropriate fonts in our plots can make them more readable and visually appealing.
- They may be mandated for publication in some journals, and for publications by organizations.
- Using `sysfonts` , and `showtext` allows us to use a wide variety of fonts from Google, making it easy to customize our plots.

## Conclusions

In this module, we have learned how to use custom fonts in our ggplot2 plots using the `showtext` package.

### Option: Adding local fonts from your computer

Using Google fonts as shown above may not be acceptable in all design projects. Using this method typically make your website non-compliant with GDPR (see below). 

::: callout-important
### GDPR Compliance
Using fonts that are already installed on your computer, or hosted on your own web server, is [**GDPR compliant**](https://gdpr-info.eu/). Using fonts *directly* from Google may not be, as it may involve sending data to Google servers every time your website is loaded by a visitor. When a visitor opens the page, their browser contacts Google, transmitting their IP address and user-agent information. Under GDPR, IP addresses are personal data, and a German court held in 2022 that dynamically loading Google Fonts without consent can breach the GDPR.


:::

One solution is to download fonts [***a priori***]{style="background-color:yellow;"} from Google, or from elsewhere, store them inside your R Project, and then import them into your session. The `sysfonts::font_add()` function allows us to do this. You will need to provide the path to the font files on your computer. That is our next step.

Let's assume we have gone off to [Google Fonts](https://fonts.google.com/) and downloaded the following fonts :`Alegreya`,`Anton`, `Roboto Condensed`, `Schoolbell`, `Tangerine`, and `Ibarra Real Nova`.

These font files are placed at `<project root>/fonts/`, i.e. a `fonts` folder at the root our our project. 

A code chunk to add these fonts to our R session as follows, using the `{{here}}` package: this code chunk can of course be pasted into the `_setup.qmd` as before, which can be invoked in each Quarto also as before. 

```{{r}}
#| label: add-local-fonts


## Clean the slate
systemfonts::clear_local_fonts()
systemfonts::clear_registry()
##
showtext_opts(dpi = 96) # set DPI for showtext

# First Add the Fonts
sysfonts::font_add(
  family = "Alegreya",
  regular = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Regular.ttf"),
  bold = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Bold.ttf"),
  italic = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Italic.ttf"),
  bolditalic = here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-BoldItalic.ttf")
)
sysfonts::font_add(
  family = "Anton",
  regular = here::here("fonts", "Anton-Regular.ttf")
) # Only one style is available
sysfonts::font_add(
  family = "RobotoCondensed",
  regular = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-Regular.ttf"),
  bold = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-Bold.ttf"),
  italic = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-Italic.ttf"),
  bolditalic = here::here("fonts", "RobotoCondensed-BoldItalic.ttf")
)
sysfonts::font_add(
  family = "IbarraNova",
  regular = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-Regular.ttf"),
  bold = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-Bold.ttf"),
  italic = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-Italic.ttf"),
  bolditalic = here::here("fonts", "IbarraRealNova-BoldItalic.ttf")
)
sysfonts::font_add(
  family = "Tangerine",
  regular = here::here("fonts", "Tangerine-Regular.ttf"),
  bold = here::here("fonts", "Tangerine-Bold.ttf")
) # only these two are available
sysfonts::font_add(
  family = "Schoolbell",
  regular = here::here("fonts", "Schoolbell-Regular.ttf")
) # Only regular is available

## Enable these fonts
showtext_auto() # set these fonts as default for the session

## Optional Check, comment out this line in production code
sysfonts::font_families() # check which fonts are available in the session

```

A couple of things worth knowing about the `{here}` package in R:

- `here::here("fonts", "Alegreya-Regular.ttf")` **builds a path from your project root** (wherever here finds a `.Rproj`, `.here` file, or `.git` folder), not from the current script's location. So the fonts folder should just be `<project root>/fonts/`.
- If your fonts folder isn't actually at the project root, adjust the first argument(s) accordingly, e.g. `here::here("assets", "fonts", "Alegreya-Regular.ttf")` if it's nested under `assets/` for example.
- If you don't already have a .here marker or RStudio project file at the root you want here to anchor to, run `here::set_here()` once from that directory, or just open the project as an RStudio Project (.Rproj), which `{here}` will detect automatically.

## Using `{ggtext}`

From [Claus Wilke's website](https://wilkelab.org/ggtext/) → www.wilkelab.org/ggtext

> The `ggtext` package provides simple Markdown and HTML rendering for ggplot2. Under the hood, the package uses the `gridtext` package for the actual rendering, and consequently it is limited to the feature set provided by `gridtext`.  
Support is provided for Markdown both in theme elements (plot titles, subtitles, captions, axis labels, legends, etc.) and in geoms (similar to `geom_text()`). In both cases, there are two alternatives, one for creating simple text labels and one for creating text boxes with word wrapping.

NOTE: on some machines, the ggtext package may not work as expected. In this case, please do as follows, using your Console:

- remove gridtext: `remove.packages(gridtext)`.   
- Install development version of `gridtext`: `remotes::install_github("wilkelab/gridtext")`

### `element_markdown()`

We can use our familiar markdown syntax right inside the titles and captions of the plot. `element_markdown()` is a theming command made available by the `ggtext` package. 

`element_markdown()` → formatted text elements, e.g. titles, caption, axis text, striptext

```{r}
#| label: ggtext-element-markdown
#| 
## Set the theme
ggplot2::theme_set(new = theme_custom())

p1 + 
  
  ## New code starts here: Two Step Procedure with ggtext
  ## 1. Markdown formatting of labels and title, using asterisks
  labs(
    title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins (*Pygoscelis*)',
    subtitle = 'A scatter plot of bill depth versus bill length.',
    caption = 'Data: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014) *PLoS ONE*',
    x = '**Bill Length** (mm)', 
    y = '**Bill Depth** (mm)',
    color = 'Body mass (g)'
  ) +
   
  ## 2. Add theme related commands from ggtext
  ## render respective text elements
  theme(
    plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown()
  )


```

### `element_markdown()` in combination with HTML

This allows us to change fonts and font-effects in titles, labels, and captions:


```{r}
## use HTML syntax to change text color
p1 + 
  labs(title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins <i style="color:#28A87D;">Pygoscelis</i>') +
  theme(
    plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10)) 
  
## use HTML syntax to change font and text size
## 
p1 + 
 labs(title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins <b style="font-size:32pt;font-family:Tangerine;">Pygoscelis</b>') +
  theme(
    plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10)) 

```

:::
